sections.title: SL-01: LMS, batch gradients, stochastic gradients

keyTerms.definition: Least mean squares: gradient descent on the squared error.
Steps downhill on the cost's slope.
Averages the slope over all examples before stepping.
Steps on one example at a time.
Alpha, the step size; too large overshoots.
The cost J is convex, so one minimum exists.

recall.question: What is the LMS update for one example?
recall.answer: theta_j := theta_j + alpha * (y^{(i)} - h_theta(x^{(i)})) * x_j^{(i)}. The step scales with the error and the feature value.

recall.question: How do batch and stochastic differ in cost per step?
recall.answer: Batch costs O(mn) per step with one step per pass. Stochastic costs O(n) per step with m steps per pass.

recall.question: Why does stochastic gradient descent never fully settle?
recall.answer: It oscillates around the minimum. Shrinking alpha to zero over time fixes the oscillation.

sections.title: SL-02: Normal equations and the projection reading

keyTerms.definition: X^T X theta = X^T y, the closed-form least-squares solution.
X theta is the shadow y casts onto the column space of X.
y - X theta, orthogonal to every feature at the optimum.
X^T X, symmetric by construction.

recall.question: What is the projection reading of least squares?
recall.answer: The prediction X theta is the shadow the target y casts onto the column space of X: the closest point, so the residuals stick straight out of the space.

recall.question: What is the strongest correctness check?
recall.answer: Residual orthogonality: X^T (y - X theta) must be near zero.

recall.question: When do the normal equations win over gradient descent?
recall.answer: When n is small, below a few thousand, and m is large: forming X^T X costs O(m n^2) and solving costs O(n^3).

sections.title: SL-03: Rank deficiency, pseudoinverse, conditioning, stable solves

keyTerms.definition: Some dial does nothing new; infinite settings give the same predictions.
The Moore-Penrose inverse picking the minimum-norm least-squares solution.
kappa = lambda_max / lambda_min; scales noise amplification.
theta = lstsq(X, y), never forming X^T X.

recall.question: What breaks when two features are identical?
recall.answer: X^T X is singular, the inverse does not exist, and the normal-equation formula breaks.

recall.question: What is the preferred order of stable solves?
recall.answer: Standardize features then use the normal equations; QR via lstsq; SVD/pseudoinverse; ridge.

recall.question: Why never ship inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y?
recall.answer: On a kappa = 1e12 matrix theta comes out as garbage with huge entries: correct math, bad numerics.

keyTerms.definition: Choosing theta to maximize the probability of the observed data.
The belief that errors follow N(0, sigma^2).
The log of the likelihood; maximizing it recovers least squares.
The noise belief giving the absolute-error objective.

recall.question: Why squared error?
recall.answer: It is the consequence of one specific belief: the errors are Gaussian noise. Maximum likelihood then hands you least squares.

recall.question: Does sigma^2 affect the chosen theta?
recall.answer: No. Sigma^2 never enters the choice of theta.

recall.question: What noise belief gives absolute error?
recall.answer: Laplace noise, p(eps) ~ exp(-|eps|/b). It resists outliers but has no closed form.

keyTerms.definition: A bump centered at x with width tau, weighting nearby points more.
Tau, the one knob controlling neighborhood width.
Dial count grows with the data; the training set is kept at prediction time.
Fixed dial count chosen before seeing data; theta is the whole model.
theta = (X^T W X)^{-1} X^T W y with W = diag(w).

recall.question: What happens at small versus large tau?
recall.answer: Small tau: only close neighbors matter, the fit wiggles. Large tau: all points count nearly equally, the fit is the global line.

recall.question: What goes wrong when querying far from all data?
recall.answer: Every weight is near zero, X^T W X is near-singular, and the prediction is garbage with high confidence. Check the weight sum.

recall.question: How do parametric and nonparametric models differ after fitting?
recall.answer: Parametric: fixed dial count, theta is the whole model, data can be thrown away. Nonparametric: dial count grows with data, training set kept at prediction time.

keyTerms.definition: The class cannot bend enough; both train and test error are high.
The class bends to the noise; train error low, test error high.

recall.question: What are typical numbers for the degree-5 fit on six noisy points?
recall.answer: Train MSE 0.00, test MSE 2.4. The train score is a lie about the future.

recall.question: What is the central trap of the whole unit?
recall.answer: Judging by train error alone always picks the most complex model.

keyTerms.definition: theta_j := theta_j + alpha * (y^{(i)} - h_theta(x^{(i)})) * x_j^{(i)}.
X^T X theta = X^T y, requiring X^T X to be invertible.
Fewer independent examples than features, or dependent features.
w^{(i)} = exp(-(x^{(i)} - x)^2 / (2 tau^2)); tau sets the neighborhood width.

recall.question: What does E03 ask?
recall.answer: What X^T (y - X theta) = 0 says in words.

recall.question: What does E09 describe?
recall.answer: After adding a feature in meters alongside feet, theta entries blow up to 1e7 and -1e7. Diagnose and fix.

recall.question: What does E12 ask for?
recall.answer: Write lwlr_predict for vector x and verify the tau -> infinity limit equals lstsq on the same data.

keyTerms.definition: A claim an experiment can disprove, here about test error versus tau.
Falling then rising, with the minimum at an interior point.

recall.question: What is the falsifiable claim?
recall.answer: Test error is U-shaped in tau, minimized at an interior point, and the minimizer moves right as noise grows.
